Sign pair: results 0.0 and 2.0, tests sign handling and exact arithmetic on both sides.
Extreme magnitudes plus zero: 1/x underflows to 0 for huge x, and division by zero for 0.
Documented example from the spec: pins the exact expected outputs including 0.91666666.
Subnormal min and max double: 1/x overflows to inf for subnormals, tests extreme FP edge cases.
Empty vector: loop body never executes, catches off-by-one with i <= x.size()-1 (size_t underflow).
Single zero element: minimal non-empty case, 0*0=0, catches skipping first/last element.
INT_MIN: most negative value, squaring overflows int, tests overflow behavior.
Both INT_MAX and INT_MIN: overflow on both elements, tests extreme value handling.
Sign handling with small odd size: negative, zero, positive, all produce distinct squares.
Duplicate equal elements (0, 0): tests that each element is squared independently.
Just over overflow threshold: 46341^2 exceeds INT_MAX, 46340^2 does not, tests boundary overflow.
Small even size with ascending values: catches off-by-one errors in loop bounds.
Empty input tests loop bounds: candidate must handle zero iterations without out-of-bounds access.
Zero value: without the x > 0 guard, 0 & (0-1) = 0 & -1 = 0 would yield a false positive.
INT_MIN: bit pattern 0x80000000 has a single bit set and x-1 overflows to INT_MAX, so only the x > 0 check prevents a false positive.
INT_MIN and INT_MAX alternating: tests sign handling and overflow at both extremes of the int range simultaneously.
All powers of two from 2^0 to 2^6: every element must return true, covering the positive branch exhaustively for small exponents.
Zero and 2^n-1 values: all have multiple bits set (or are zero), must all return false, catching off-by-one in the bit trick.
Negative, zero, and smallest power of two in one vector: three sign-boundary cases that exercise the x > 0 short-circuit in sequence.
Duplicate adjacent elements: tests that each element is processed independently with no erroneous caching or deduplication.
Documented example from the function comment: verifies the candidate matches the reference on the canonical non-singular case with exact expected output [[4,3],[1.5,-1.5]].

Symmetric positive-definite matrix with negative off-diagonals: exercises sign handling in factor=A[i][k]/A[k][k] and the subtraction update A[i][j]-=factor*A[k][j] where a candidate might flip += and -=.

Upper-triangular 3×3 matrix: every sub-diagonal element is zero so all factors are 0 and the matrix must pass through unchanged—exposes candidates that corrupt the upper triangle via off-by-one in the j-loop bound.
Every cell is a corner with exactly 2 neighbors equal to 1, testing that count==1 correctly rejects count==2.
Interior cell (1,1) has all four neighbor directions checked and exactly one is 1, exercising the full 4-neighbor path.
Nonzero non-one values (2 and -1) must not be counted, distinguishing ==1 from !=0 implementations.
The documented example with known answer, covering corners, edges, and interior simultaneously.
Single 1 at corner (0,0): center cell (1,1) has zero orthogonal neighbors but one diagonal, distinguishing 4-connected from 8-connected.
All-corner 2x2 image where pixel(0,0) sum=8*32=256 exceeds 255, testing upper clip boundary and boundary handling.
Pixel(0,0) sum=8*0-1=-1 just below zero, testing lower clip boundary at the exact threshold between clipping and not.
Uniform 3x3 image where center sum=0 (8*32-8*32) and corners sum=160, testing kernel weight correctness and sign handling.
Spike at center produces sum=2040 (clipped to 255) while edge neighbors produce negative sums (clipped to 0), testing both clip directions in one image.
Smallest even grid where every cell is a corner with only two neighbors plus self, exposing division-by-count vs division-by-5 bugs.
Matches the documented example exactly, validating corner, edge, and interior cells against the spec.
A dead corner with exactly 3 live neighbors becomes alive; tests corner neighbor bounds and the dead-cell birth branch.
2x2 block still life: every live cell has exactly 3 neighbors and survives; tests survival with sum==3 on an all-corner grid.
Vertical blinker becomes horizontal; tests exact 2/3 survival and dead-cell birth with exactly 3 neighbors.
All alive grid: corners survive with 3, edges/center die with >3; tests the >3 branch and bounded vs wrap-around neighbor counting.
Checkerboard pattern depends on diagonal neighbor accumulation; missing diagonals changes births and survival.
A negative non-1 cell is dead but contributes -1 to neighbor sums; targets the ==1 liveness check and sign handling in the sum.
Empty input triggers the size < 3 base case; a candidate that omits this guard would access invalid indices.
Two points is the boundary of the size < 3 base case; tests that the candidate does not enter the main hull algorithm.
Three identical points: cross product is always 0, causing the while loops to pop all intermediate points in both upper and lower hulls.
Three distinct collinear points: cross product is 0 but points differ, testing collinear removal without degenerate duplicates.
Alternating numeric_limits lowest/max values can cause overflow to inf in cross product subtractions, testing numerical robustness.
Nearly sorted input with one swap; the reference re-sorts, but a candidate that assumes pre-sorted input would produce a different hull.
Duplicate adjacent values create zero-length segments; cross product with identical points yields 0, testing duplicate handling in hull construction.
Seven identical points at midpoint: larger odd-sized degenerate input that exercises more loop iterations with always-zero cross products.
N=0 causes unsigned underflow: N-1 wraps to SIZE_MAX, making the elimination loop iterate out of bounds.
Base case: elimination loop is skipped (0 < 0 false), back substitution performs a single division by A[0].
Minimal case exercising exactly one elimination iteration and two back-substitution steps.
Matches the documented example size; odd N tests the full elimination and back-substitution chain.
All-zero matrix hits the pivot==0 early-return branch on the first elimination iteration.
Small odd size > 3 to test deeper elimination chains and back-substitution accumulation.
Large N with extreme values risks floating-point overflow in factor*A_copy during elimination.
Division by zero in M_PI/N and 1/x.size(); log2(0) yields undefined behavior in the bit-reversal stage.
Single-element input: the while-loop is skipped and the bit-reversal shift >> (32-0) is undefined behavior.
Smallest power-of-two: exercises exactly one butterfly stage and a single bit-reversal swap.
Non-power-of-two size: the butterfly halving and log2-based bit-reversal assume a power of two, producing incorrect or platform-dependent results.
All-ones input: the IDFT should yield a unit impulse at index 0, testing conjugation of real values and 1/N scaling.
Alternating numeric_limits lowest/max: butterfly additions and subtractions overflow to inf or nan, exposing floating-point edge handling.
Adjacent duplicate elements after random fill: tests symmetry and equal-value subtraction (x[a]-x[b]=0) in the butterfly.
Larger power-of-two with sign alternation: exercises four butterfly stages and bit-reversal with m=4, testing twiddle-factor accumulation.
Targets division by zero in thetaT = PI/N where N=0 and undefined behavior in log2(0) cast to unsigned int.
Exposes undefined behavior from log2(1)=0 producing m=0, causing >>32 shift in bit reversal decimation.
Smallest meaningful FFT; tests butterfly with zero differences (x[a]-x[b]=0) when all elements are equal.
Tests overflow in butterfly subtraction where lowest-max produces -inf and lowest+max produces zero.
Tests sign handling in butterfly additions and subtractions with alternating positive and negative inputs.
Example size with zero input; verifies zero-in zero-out property without spurious NaN or inf from twiddle factors.
Larger power-of-2 with varying magnitudes; tests conjugate correctness with many complex frequency components.
Larger power-of-2; tests precision accumulation from repeated phiT squaring across multiple butterfly stages.
N=0 causes division by zero in thetaT = pi/N and undefined log2(0) in decimation.
N=1 yields m=log2(1)=0, making bit-reversal shift by 32 bits (undefined behavior) and exercises the trivial base case.
Single non-zero element: the while loop is skipped entirely, testing that the candidate handles the degenerate transform correctly.
Smallest power-of-2 that enters the butterfly loop; all-zero input exposes sign and zero-multiplication handling.
Non-power-of-two size violates the algorithm's implicit assumption; k=3>>1=1 truncates, m=log2(3)=1 misaligns bit-reversal, exposing divergence from a candidate that validates size.
Small power-of-two with a linear ramp exercises one full butterfly level and decimation with m=2, catching off-by-one in combine/swap logic.
Alternating numeric_limits lowest/max causes catastrophic cancellation and potential overflow in x_copy[a] += x_copy[b] and complex multiply.
Two identical huge values: x_copy[a] += x_copy[b] produces 2e308 which overflows to inf, testing overflow propagation through the butterfly.
Empty graph (N=0): exposes size_t underflow in `N-1` loop bounds and empty-vector indexing in candidate implementations.
Single-node graph: an off-by-one using `j < N-1` with signed N would skip the only element, yielding count 0 instead of the correct value.
Smallest non-trivial even matrix: boundary case for 2×2 row-major indexing `i*N+j` and double-loop nesting.
Small odd dimension: catches asymmetric loop-bound bugs that only manifest on odd N (e.g., `j < N` vs `j <= N-1` edge interactions).
Matches the documented example dimension (4×4), validating the canonical case and row-major stride of 4.
Medium odd size: stresses index arithmetic `i*N+j` at scale where int-vs-size_t multiplication differences could surface.
Maximum allowed size (N²=16,777,216 elements): tests large-loop iteration counts and whether candidate index variables overflow or truncate.
Empty graph with N=0: tests loop base case where no vertices exist and maxCount remains 0
Single vertex with no self-loop: tests DFS base case, count=1, and minimal component return
Smallest non-trivial graph: tests edge detection between two vertices and component merging logic
Small odd-sized graph: tests component counting with potential for isolated vertices or multiple small components
Small even-sized graph matching the example: validates basic component detection on typical input
Moderate size: tests recursion depth in DFS which could cause stack overflow with chain-like graph structures
Maximum allowed size: tests deep recursion, large index computation (node*N+i), and performance limits
Empty graph (N=0): tests base case where no loop iterations execute and maxDegree stays initialized at 0.
Single-node graph (N=1): tests minimal N*N=1 element matrix, single-row degree sum, and diagonal element inclusion.
Smallest multi-node graph (N=2): tests even N with 2x2 row-major indexing and inter-node edge counting.
Small odd N=3: tests odd-dimensioned matrix stride and degree accumulation across non-power-of-two rows.
Small odd prime N=7: tests non-power-of-two row-major index arithmetic i*N+j with larger stride.
Large even power-of-two N=1024: stress-tests index calculation and degree accumulation at scale where int overflow in sums becomes plausible.
Maximum allowed N=4096: tests large-scale row-major indexing, potential int overflow in degree sums, and loop bound comparison int vs size_t.
Empty graph (N=0): loop never executes, tests zero-size vector allocation and empty-input return value.
Single node (N=1): minimal DFS base case with no recursive calls, tests single-element graph counting.
Two-node graph (N=2): smallest non-trivial case where an edge may or may not exist, tests off-by-one in adjacency indexing.
Three-node graph (N=3): small odd dimension testing triangle connectivity and multi-level DFS recursion.
Five-node graph (N=5): small prime dimension testing component counting with multiple possible sub-graphs.
32-node graph (N=32): medium even size testing DFS recursion depth and visited-array scaling.
64-node graph (N=64): maximum allowed size, stresses recursion depth and performance on large adjacency matrix.
N=0 empty graph: visited[source] on empty vector is UB, testing crash-safety and base-case handling.
N=1 single node: source==dest==0 triggers immediate return of 0 before any neighbor loop, testing the trivial base case.
N=2 minimal non-trivial graph: tests the smallest case where an edge traversal (pathLength+1) can occur.
Small odd N: tests loop bound i<N with a non-power-of-two iteration count and potential 2-hop path.
N=4 matches the documented example graph size, exercising a multi-hop BFS with branching factor >1.
Medium-large N: tests that pathLength accumulation across many BFS levels does not overflow int and queue operations scale.
Maximum allowed N: stress-tests loop bounds (i<N with large N), visited array allocation, and adjacency indexing current*N+i for overflow in size_t arithmetic.
Empty vector: loop must not execute, tests zero-iteration boundary and prevents out-of-bounds access on s[0].
Single element: minimal non-empty case; exposes off-by-one if candidate uses <= instead of < or subtracts 1 from size as loop bound.
Two elements: classic off-by-one boundary where a candidate using i <= s.size()-1 with unsigned underflow would be exposed.
Small odd size: ensures loop iterates correctly for odd counts without premature termination at even boundaries.
Size exactly equals bins array length (26): boundary where a candidate might confuse vector size with bins array size.
One more than bins array length: ensures no aliasing or confusion between input vector size and the 26-element output array.
Maximum allowed size: stresses accumulation in bins counters and exposes overflow if candidate uses narrower integer types for counts.
Empty vector: std::reduce must return the initial value false without ever invoking the XOR lambda.
Single element: reduce folds init(false) op element exactly once; tests no-loop / single-step path.
Smallest multi-element even size: exactly one binary op call; off-by-one in loop bounds would miscount.
Smallest odd count: parity of true values determines result; even-vs-odd handling bugs surface here.
Small odd prime size: non-power-of-two element count may expose uneven parallel chunking in std::reduce.
Just below a power of two: boundary where parallel reduce chunk-splitting off-by-one errors appear.
Exact power of two: likely triggers the parallel reduce fast path with perfectly balanced chunks.
Empty vectors test std::find on empty range where begin==end, ensuring no dereference or size-based loop issues.
Single-element vectors test minimal non-empty search; both containers share the same value, exercising the in-both (false) branch.
Duplicate elements with narrow range increase probability val appears in exactly one container, testing duplicate handling and the XOR-true branch.
INT_MIN/INT_MAX alternating values test sign handling and equality comparison at numeric extremes.
Small odd size with reverse-sorted data catches candidate implementations that incorrectly assume sorted input and use binary search.
Large vector with spike at last index tests full linear scan to the end, catching early-termination or off-by-one loop bugs.
All-zero vectors with val=0 test the in-both (false) case and catch short-circuit implementations that return true after finding val in x only.
Nearly sorted data with one swapped pair catches binary search assumptions while still having mostly ordered elements.
Empty vector base case: sort of zero elements must not crash or access memory.
Single-element vector: no comparisons should be needed, must return unchanged.
INT_MIN/INT_MAX startTime pair: catches overflow in subtraction-based comparators (a.startTime - b.startTime).
All equal startTimes: comparator must return false for both orderings, testing strict-weak-ordering compliance.
Minimal two-element reverse pair: exactly one swap needed, tests off-by-one in comparison direction.
Fully reversed input: worst-case for many sort implementations, exposes O(n^2) degradation or incorrect partitioning.
Adjacent duplicate startTimes at index 3: tests that equal elements are handled without infinite loops or data corruption.
Empty vector: loops execute zero times, exposes off-by-one and empty-range bugs in collection/sort/writeback.
Single element: minimal non-empty case, tests single-iteration writeback and index increment.
All zeros with even size: nonZeroElements stays empty, verifies no writes occur and zero positions are preserved.
Two-element descending pair: smallest sort case, exposes swap/order bugs and boundary indexing.
Small odd size with mixed signs: tests sign handling in sort and odd-length writeback loop bounds.
Odd size with INT lowest/max: targets overflow/underflow and extreme-value comparison behavior in std::sort.
Power-of-two size all zeros: combines all-zero path with even size, stressing empty nonZeroElements writeback.
Large even size with random signed values: stress test for index tracking, duplicate handling, and full writeback coverage.
Empty matrices test loop bounds and Y.assign(M*N,0) with no iterations.
Single non-zero element in each matrix tests the minimal one-pair multiplication path.
Duplicate COO elements (same row/col/value) test += accumulation to the same Y cell.
Alternating numeric_limits lowest/max values test overflow and inf in a.value * x.value.
Ramp from negative to positive tests sign handling in multiplication across matching pairs.
Nearly-sorted COO with one swap exposes implementations that incorrectly assume sorted input for merge-join.
Spike to max/2 in one element tests overflow when multiplied by another non-trivial value.
N=0 base case: no loop iterations, tests empty matrix handling and output vector sizing.
N=1 minimal case: single element, no division path executed, tests diagonal L[i*N+i]=1 assignment.
Zero pivot at U[0][0]=0 causes 0/0=NaN in L[1][0] division, testing division-by-zero behavior.
All-ones matrix produces zero pivot at U[1][1]=0, causing inf in L[2][1] division for N>=3.
Alternating lowest/max values cause overflow in L*U products and inf/NaN propagation through subtraction.
Negative values in matrix test sign handling in L and U computation, especially in subtraction steps.
Simple 2x2 matrix with known LU decomposition, tests basic correctness of the factorization algorithm.
N=4 even size tests loop bounds and k<i, k<j conditions with multiple iterations of the inner subtraction loops.
